how_they_meet: Raja knocks down Kajal's mother-in-law Lakshmi Devi with his motorcycle, takes her home and meets Kajal.
courtship_pattern: Raja declares his love; Kajal cuts him short and reveals she is a widow. He returns with his suit, she keeps resisting, and he wins over her mother-in-law, who persuades Kajal to accept. Kajal realises she loves him only after he is hospitalised in an accident.
emotional_dynamic: His ardent persistence against her grief and reluctance, turning to mutual love after his accident
pair_conflict: Kajal's refusal to remarry and Raja's refusal to accept it.
pair_friction_explanation: Kajal repeatedly rejects Raja, a sustained but non-hostile disagreement. Once she admits her love there is no documented conflict, and she chooses to stay with him when Ravi returns.
external_opposition_explanation: Raja's father opposes a widow bride and throws him out; Kajal's first husband Ravi returns alive; Dhirendra kidnaps the couple and straps a bomb to Kajal, ending in Dhirendra's and Ravi's deaths.
lover_boy_explanation: Romance is Raja's overriding motive: he gives up his family's wealth to marry Kajal. A contemporary review described the role as 'a young man obsessed with love', and it launched Khan's romantic career.
chemistry_explanation: Anupama Chopra (2007) wrote that Bharti matched Khan's manic intensity 'emotion to emotion', and contemporary reviews singled out both performances. Interpretive score.
actor_transformation: From carefree rich son to a self-supporting husband who runs a garage.
female_transformation: From grieving widow to a woman who accepts remarriage and chooses her second husband over her returned first husband.
relationship_outcome: Married; they survive Dhirendra's plot and honour Ravi's sacrifice.
relationship_analysis: Deewana presents Raja's persistence as devotion that overcomes the stigma of widow remarriage. His refusal to take no for an answer is rewarded, and Kajal's consent comes through her mother-in-law's persuasion before she feels love herself. Ravi's return tests the marriage, but Kajal's loyalty is not in doubt, so the real obstacles are external: a disapproving father and a greedy villain.
critical_reading: Contemporary reviewers saw a fresh take on the lover obsessed with love, and the film is regarded as an early treatment of widow remarriage. A modern reading credits the progressive theme but notes that the heroine's refusals are overridden by male persistence and family persuasion.

critical_reading: No contemporary reading of the pair was found. A modern reading sees a film that centres female desire and dissatisfaction, with the young lover as an unreliable escape.

how_they_meet: Not documented.

critical_reading: No contemporary reading of the pair was found. A modern reading notes that the heroine's agency comes from seeing through the romance rather than from the romance itself.

how_they_meet: They were classmates; the film opens with Rahul already obsessed with her.

emotional_dynamic: Kiran's fear and refusal against Rahul's escalating possessiveness
pair_conflict: Kiran rejects Rahul and loves Sunil; Rahul refuses to accept it.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no relationship, only stalking, violence and an attempted forced marriage; Kiran consistently rejects Rahul's claim on her.
external_opposition_explanation: Kiran's engagement and marriage to Sunil, her brother's family and police protection stand between Rahul and Kiran; Sunil finally shoots him.
lover_boy_explanation: Obsessive love is Rahul's overwhelming motive, but the film frames him as a stalker and villain, not a romantic hero; the intensity is captured by romance centrality instead.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing; the article reports that Khan's obsessive lover was widely appreciated. The pair share pursuit rather than romance, and the charge comes from Khan's performance against Chawla's credible fear rather than from mutual interplay.
actor_transformation: Dying, he expresses shame and begs Kiran not to hate him.
female_transformation: From fear to resistance: she rejects his authority, locks herself away and feigns agreement to survive.
relationship_outcome: Sunil shoots Rahul dead; Kiran and Sunil return to India.
relationship_analysis: Darr splits the romantic hero in two: Sunil is the sanctioned lover and Rahul the obsessive one, and the film's force comes from giving the obsessive lover the charisma and the stammered 'I love you, K-k-k-Kiran'. The pair never forms a relationship; Kiran's story is one of surviving pursuit.
critical_reading: Khan's portrayal of an obsessive lover was widely appreciated by critics and audiences, and his stammered line became iconic. A modern reading treats the role as a portrait of stalking and coercion whose star appeal risks romanticising the stalker.

how_they_meet: They already play in the same six-member band; Anna rejoins it after time away.

emotional_dynamic: Sunil's devoted but self-serving love against Anna's steady love for Chris
pair_conflict: Sunil's lies to separate Anna and Chris.
pair_friction_explanation: Sunil's deliberate lies provoke Anna's fury: she slaps him and refuses to speak to him. The rift heals, but her love for Chris keeps them at odds with his hopes.
external_opposition_explanation: Anna and Chris love each other; Anna's father briefly favours Sunil only after Chris's parents fix another marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Winning Anna is Sunil's defining motive alongside music, and his arc ends in romantic self-sacrifice; he is the film's romantic hero even though he loses.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The friendship scenes are warm and teasing, but Anna's affection is for Chris, so the rapport is real only as companionship and the film's appeal rests on Khan's lovable loser.
actor_transformation: From a jealous schemer to a man who reunites Anna with Chris at the cost of his own hopes.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond her consistent choice of Chris.
relationship_outcome: Anna marries Chris; Sunil is heartbroken, then meets a new girl.
relationship_analysis: The film tells a conventional triangle from the losing lover's side. Sunil's lies make him the obstacle to Anna and Chris, yet the film keeps him sympathetic and resolves his arc through self-sacrifice: he reunites the couple and wavers only once, over the dropped ring. It sets out the lovable loser who wins the audience rather than the girl.
critical_reading: Sampada Sharma (The Indian Express) observed that told conventionally this would be Chris and Anna's love story with Sunil as the villain; Kundan Shah instead makes him the hero, with subtle, circumstantial humour. A modern reading credits the film for letting the hero lose while noting that his deception is forgiven because it is charming.

how_they_meet: Vijay, a wealthy industrialist, meets Shivani, an Air India air hostess, and is instantly infatuated.
courtship_pattern: He tries to hire her as a model, pursues her and seeks her hand; after her marriage he befriends and employs her husband, uses her photographs in advertisements, kills her husband, frames her for attempted murder and repeatedly demands that she say she loves him.
emotional_dynamic: Vijay's possessive entitlement against Shivani's refusal and eventual vengeance
pair_conflict: Shivani's rejection and Vijay's violent obsession.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no relationship, only persecution: Vijay kills her husband, beats and frames her, and causes her sister's and daughter's deaths; she finally kills him.
external_opposition_explanation: Shivani's marriage to Ashok stands between Vijay and his goal; Inspector Arjun, bribed by Vijay, works for him rather than against him.
lover_boy_explanation: Obsession drives Vijay, but the film makes him its antagonist; he has none of the lover boy's devotion or openness.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The interaction is antagonism, not romance; Dixit's loathing and Khan's mania make the confrontations forceful, but there is no attraction for the audience to believe in from her side.
actor_transformation: Paralysed after the accident, he is nursed back to health by Shivani and still demands her love.
female_transformation: From air hostess and mother to a hardened avenger who kills her persecutors and dies taking Vijay with her.
relationship_outcome: Shivani stabs Vijay and lets go on a cliff edge, and both fall to their deaths.
relationship_analysis: Anjaam pushes the Darr template further by making the pursued woman the protagonist and giving her the revenge plot. Vijay's obsession destroys her husband, sister, daughter and unborn child, and the film treats her violence as justice. Of Khan's early negative roles, this is the one least sympathetic to the obsessive lover.
critical_reading: The film is described as being about a woman facing the brunt of her obsessive lover and the atrocities committed against women, with Dixit as protagonist and Khan as antagonist. A modern reading sees an explicit critique of male entitlement, delivered through lurid revenge melodrama.

how_they_meet: At the start of a backpacking trip across Europe, Raj helps a late Simran board a moving train.
courtship_pattern: Raj's flirting annoys Simran, but their groups keep meeting until the two miss a train and travel alone; they open up, and Simran falls in love. Raj follows her to Punjab, poses as her fiancé's friend and wins over her family while refusing to elope.
emotional_dynamic: Playful flirtation becomes deep mutual love; Raj's patience against Simran's filial duty
pair_conflict: Initial annoyance at Raj's flirting; later, Raj's refusal to elope without her father's blessing.
pair_friction_explanation: Early irritation is playful, and from the journey onward the couple is aligned; the only strain is their powerlessness before Simran's father.
external_opposition_explanation: Simran has been betrothed since childhood to Kuljeet; her father Baldev dictates her life, violently throws Raj out when he learns the truth, and Kuljeet's men ambush Raj at the station.
lover_boy_explanation: The defining lover-boy role: romance organises Raj's every action, from following Simran to India to insisting on her father's consent; a reviewer said Khan redefined 'the Lover for the 1990s'.
chemistry_explanation: Anupama Chopra (NDTV) credited 'the magic of Shah Rukh Khan and Kajol who created a template for modern love, which was hip and cool but resolutely Indian'. Interpretive score.
actor_transformation: From a brash, flirtatious young man with an unsettled view of life to a devoted suitor who will marry only with the family's blessing.
female_transformation: From a dutiful daughter who silently endures Kuljeet to a woman who begs her father to let her be with the man she loves.
relationship_outcome: Baldev relents at the station and Simran runs to board Raj's train.
relationship_analysis: DDLJ fuses the diaspora hero's modern mobility with filial obedience: Raj wins Simran not by eloping but by earning her father's consent, and the film makes that refusal its moral centre. The lovers are aligned from the European journey onward, so nearly all conflict is external, from Baldev's childhood promise to Kuljeet's violence. Simran's choices are limited to pleading, which invites a modern reading of the romance as both liberating and conservative.
critical_reading: Anupama Chopra saw a romance of innocence in which Raj 'understands the importance of an Indian woman's honor' and a milestone that shaped 1990s Hindi cinema. A modern reading notes that the heroine's happiness depends on her father's permission and that the hero's respect for tradition is part of his appeal.

pair_friction_explanation: Bela refuses to elope and grows to dislike Ram Jaane's criminality, a recurring clash of values rather than open hostility.
external_opposition_explanation: Bela and Murli secretly love each other, and Ram Jaane's crimes lead to his death sentence.
lover_boy_explanation: Ram Jaane is a gangster whose love for Bela is one strand of a crime-and-redemption story.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Bela's kindness is read by Ram Jaane as love, so the two play at cross-purposes; Chawla's warmth registers, but the pairing is built to be one-sided.

female_transformation: Tries to reform Ram Jaane and comes to reject his criminality.
relationship_outcome: Ram Jaane is executed; Bela remains with Murli.
relationship_analysis: Bela is less a love interest than a moral test in the story of a nameless boy turned criminal. Ram Jaane misreads her attention as love, and his final letter recasts his loss as a deliberate sacrifice, the same redemptive gesture as feigning fear on the gallows.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found. A modern reading sees the heroine as an instrument of the hero's redemption rather than a partner.

courtship_pattern: Rahul arranges Siddharth's courtship while quietly attracted to Seema; they grow close, pose as a married couple for his heart-patient mother, argue and fall in love.

external_opposition_explanation: Siddharth wants Seema and offers Rahul his dream office in exchange; Bhushan's lie to Rahul's mother forces the pretend marriage.

chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. One of the strongest Khan and Chawla films: the comic timing between them carries the romance, and Seema's scepticism gives Chawla room to match Khan's charm rather than receive it.
actor_transformation: Stops enabling his boss, refuses the office offered in exchange for Seema and resolves to earn his own way.
female_transformation: Gives up pursuing luxury through Siddharth and chooses Rahul.
relationship_outcome: Seema chooses Rahul, and they ride off on a scooter marked 'Don't Worry, Get Married'.
relationship_analysis: A For Love or Money remake in which the romance is also the hero's moral rehabilitation: Rahul begins as his boss's paid enabler and wins Seema only by refusing the reward for giving her up. Both lovers start out chasing wealth, so their union doubles as a rejection of it.
critical_reading: K. N. Vijiyan (New Straits Times) praised a 'bubbly Shahrukh Khan at his best'. A modern reading notes that the heroine is first treated as a prize passed between men, which the ending only partly corrects.

courtship_pattern: Arjun smooths the way for Rajiv and becomes Ganga's only confidant in the US. After Rajiv's assault he escorts her home, confesses his love when accused of eloping, and is given her hand.

external_opposition_explanation: Ganga is engaged to Rajiv by her father and Kishorilal; the village accuses the pair of eloping, and Rajiv's goons attack Arjun in a fight to the death.
lover_boy_explanation: Arjun is a restrained romantic hero whose loyalty to his foster father competes with his love until the end.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; the article reports praise for Khan's and Chaudhry's performances without assessing the pairing. Arjun's restraint while Ganga is engaged keeps the romance in glances and songs, which the two play tenderly.
actor_transformation: From dutiful foster son promoting his brother's match to a man who declares his own love.
female_transformation: From a village bride chosen to 'Indianise' Rajiv to a woman who fights off her fiancé's assault and publicly exposes him.
relationship_outcome: They marry and return to the US as a couple.
relationship_analysis: Pardes turns the triangle into an allegory of good and bad diaspora Indians: loyal, culturally rooted Arjun earns Ganga, while Westernised Rajiv is exposed as abusive. Arjun never pursues her while she is engaged; his love is declared only after her ordeal.
critical_reading: Gita Rajan and Shailja Sharma (New Cosmopolitanisms) read the film as a dichotomy of the good NRI versus the bad, with Khan's Arjun a metaphor for Indian cultural nationalism. A modern reading notes that the heroine's worth is tied to her insistence on chastity.

how_they_meet: After a series of near misses marked by a recurring tune, Rahul sees Pooja dancing and persuades her to replace the injured Nisha in his musical Maya.
courtship_pattern: Rehearsals make them close friends and then lovers, but neither can say so; Pooja is already engaged to Ajay.
emotional_dynamic: Unspoken, destined love expressed through dance and music
pair_conflict: Pooja's engagement and their shared inability to declare their feelings.

external_opposition_explanation: Pooja's engagement to her childhood friend Ajay stands in the way until Ajay himself steps aside.

chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; the article reports wide praise for the performances of Khan and Dixit without assessing the pairing. The film rests on the near-misses between Rahul and Pooja, and the two sustain the yearning through its song-and-dance structure.
actor_transformation: The director of happy endings rewrites his play to end in separation when he loses Pooja, before love restores the happy ending.
female_transformation: From a conflicted fiancée to a woman who acknowledges and declares her love.
relationship_outcome: They confess their love on stage at the premiere after Ajay plays Pooja's taped confession.
relationship_analysis: Dil To Pagal Hai stages romance as destiny: a recurring tune, near misses and a musical about waiting for true love. The obstacles are gentle, a fiancé who gives way and a friend's unrequited love, so the tension is emotional hesitation rather than opposition. Khan's character articulates the film's philosophy of love.
critical_reading: Omar Ahmed (Empire, 4/5) called it 'great eye-candy' with good performances, and Screen praised Yash Chopra's sophistication. A modern reading notes that the heroine's release from her engagement depends on her fiancé's generosity.

how_they_meet: Stranded at Haflong railway station in a rainstorm, Amar is intrigued by a silent woman who asks for tea and leaves on a train before he returns.

pair_friction_explanation: She lies to him, lures him into a beating and exploits his credentials; he pursues her aggressively and confronts her. Moments of vulnerability do not bridge their opposed goals.
external_opposition_explanation: Her insurgent cell attacks Amar, the CBI arrests him as a suspect, and her handler remotely detonates her vest, killing both.
lover_boy_explanation: Love for Meghna becomes Amar's overwhelming motive and ends in his death, but the pursuit is so aggressive that the role complicates the devoted lover-boy ideal.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Khan's insistence and Koirala's guarded withdrawal produce a tense, unsettled attraction that suits the film's design, though by intention it never becomes a shared romance.
actor_transformation: From an intrigued journalist to a man who will die rather than let her go.
female_transformation: Moina, brutalised by security forces as a child, finally yields to her feelings moments before her handler detonates the vest.
relationship_outcome: Both are killed when her vest is detonated as they embrace.
relationship_analysis: Dil Se pairs romantic obsession with political violence: Amar's pursuit is persistent to the point of aggression, and Meghna's trauma and mission make her unreachable. The film unites them only in death, turning the romance into a collision between private desire and a national wound.
critical_reading: Deepa Deosthalee called the film 'a picture-perfect ode to love', while Khalid Mohamed and Anupama Chopra were cooler on its storytelling. A modern reading sees an aggressive pursuit framed as destiny, partly offset by the film's attention to the woman's political trauma.

chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; a review quoted in the article praises Kapoor's Kaurwaki as a 'lively mix of flirtatious coquette and feisty warrior woman'. The forest courtship has energy, but the disguise and the war keep the pair apart for most of the film.
actor_transformation: Believing her dead turns him brutal; finding her among the carnage he caused leads to his renunciation.
female_transformation: From fugitive princess to restored ruler of Kalinga, wounded in the war waged by the husband she knew as Pawan.
relationship_outcome: They reunite on the battlefield and Asoka apologises as Arya dies; he then renounces violence.
relationship_analysis: Asoka's first love is the hinge of the epic: the false report of Kaurwaki's death releases his cruelty, and her survival among the dead of Kalinga forces his conversion. Their marriage, built on his disguise, never becomes a shared life.
critical_reading: Peter Bradshaw praised the film's 'intricate, indirect eroticism – no sex, or even kissing'; the BBC's Santosh Sinha felt Khan the star took over from Asoka in this section. A modern reading notes that the romance serves the conqueror's redemption more than the princess's story.

how_they_meet: Devi, a Buddhist maiden, nurses the wounded Asoka at a monastery in Vidisa.
courtship_pattern: She cares for him and helps him survive an assassination attempt; they marry.
emotional_dynamic: Care and gratitude
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the couple is recorded; low score carries Low confidence.
external_opposition_explanation: Susima's assassins attack Asoka at Vidisa.
lover_boy_explanation: The marriage marks Asoka's return to power while he mourns Kaurwaki; it is not a romantic arc.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The marriage to Devi is a transition in Asoka's story, and the film gives the two little shared feeling to play.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Not documented.
relationship_outcome: Married; Asoka returns in splendour to Pataliputra.
relationship_analysis: The marriage to Devi comes while Asoka believes Kaurwaki dead and accompanies his return to power. The summary does not develop it, though Devi's Buddhism anticipates his conversion.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Not documented; Anjali is a lively young woman from Chandni Chowk.
courtship_pattern: Rahul considers ending the relationship to obey Yash, but marries Anjali after her father's sudden death.
emotional_dynamic: Dutiful husband and exuberant wife bound together by exile
pair_conflict: Rahul's duty to his father against his love.
pair_friction_explanation: Rahul's hesitation is about his father, not Anjali; the marriage is united throughout the exile.
external_opposition_explanation: Yash disapproves of Anjali's class, wants Rahul to marry Naina, and disowns him, causing a ten-year estrangement.
lover_boy_explanation: Rahul chooses love over family, but the role is defined as much by filial duty and longing for his father.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; the reviews in the article praise Kajol's performance without assessing the pairing. The Chandni Chowk courtship revives the Khan and Kajol playfulness of their earlier hits, though the family drama soon overtakes the romance.
actor_transformation: Chooses marriage over his father's approval and lives in exile until reconciliation.
female_transformation: Leaves Chandni Chowk for London as Rahul's wife and the mother of Krish.
relationship_outcome: Married with a son, Krish; the family belatedly celebrates their wedding.
relationship_analysis: The romance causes the family rupture rather than carrying the story: Yash disowns Rahul for choosing Anjali, and the emotional climax is the father's apology, not the couple's union. It reverses DDLJ, whose hero refuses to marry without the father's blessing.
critical_reading: Kajol was widely praised; The Hindu wrote that she 'steals the thunder from under very high noses'. A modern reading notes that the film treats class prejudice as a father's pride to be forgiven rather than confronted.

how_they_meet: After her mother's death Radha moves into her grandfather Dev Narayan's house, where Gopal, an orphan Dev raised, now lives.
courtship_pattern: Gopal falls in love with Radha and Dev arranges their marriage.
emotional_dynamic: A possessive husband's growing suspicion of his wife's closeness to her adoptive brother
pair_conflict: Gopal suspects Radha of an affair with Suraj.
pair_friction_explanation: Mounting misunderstandings end with Gopal throwing Radha out of the house and refusing to hear her or Suraj: a serious rupture driven by distrust.
external_opposition_explanation: Incidents on the honeymoon and Prashant's expulsion feed the suspicion, but no outsider sets out to break the marriage.
lover_boy_explanation: Gopal loves Radha, but the role is defined by jealousy and bitterness rather than romantic devotion.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The jealousy plot casts Khan as a suspicious husband, which strains the warmth that Dixit brings to the marriage.
actor_transformation: Grows angry and bitter, then realises he mistook a sibling bond for adultery and apologises.
female_transformation: Thrown out of her marital home, she is reconciled when Gopal recognises his error.
relationship_outcome: Gopal reunites with Radha and apologises to Suraj.
relationship_analysis: The film is a study in possessive jealousy: Gopal reads Radha's devotion to her adoptive brother as adultery and expels her. Reconciliation depends entirely on his change of mind; Radha's innocence never has to be proved by her.
critical_reading: Derek Elley (Variety) called the long-delayed film 'a major disappointment', and Omar Ahmed (Empire) found nothing fresh in its triangle. A modern reading sees a marriage in which male suspicion costs the husband only temporary loneliness.

how_they_meet: Inseparable childhood friends whose bond is rekindled when Devdas returns from ten years in London.
courtship_pattern: Their companionship matures into reciprocal love; Paro has kept a lamp burning for his return and secretly visits him after his family humiliates her mother.
emotional_dynamic: Deep mutual love undone by his lack of courage
pair_conflict: Devdas's cowardice before his family and his letter claiming he never loved her.
pair_friction_explanation: Devdas abandons Paro with a cruel, false letter, and she rebukes him fiercely when he tries to stop her wedding: a serious rupture caused by him, though their love persists.
external_opposition_explanation: Devdas's mother rejects Paro's lineage and humiliates her mother, his father disgraces Paro, his sister-in-law schemes, and Paro's husband finally has the gates shut as Devdas dies outside.
lover_boy_explanation: Lost love consumes Devdas's identity and destroys him, but he fails to act for it; the role is the archetypal tragic lover rather than a courting hero.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; reviewers were divided: Sheila Johnston (Screen International) thought Khan's chemistry with Rai 'a failure', while the film's admirers centred on the lovers' scenes. The grand staging sometimes overwhelms the intimacy.
actor_transformation: From a returning heir in love to a self-destructive alcoholic who dies at Paro's gate.
female_transformation: From devoted childhood sweetheart to a dutiful, confined wife who never stops loving Devdas.
relationship_outcome: Devdas dies outside Paro's marital home as the gates close on her.
relationship_analysis: Devdas is Khan's fullest portrait of romantic failure. The obstacles are real (class snobbery, a scheming sister-in-law, a patriarchal father), but the decisive rupture is his own cowardly letter. Paro keeps her dignity and her vow; he destroys himself, and the film's grandeur ennobles a love that never acts.
critical_reading: Indian reviews were mixed, praising Madhuri Dixit but divided on Khan and Rai; Ratna Rajaiah (The Hindu) called the film 'a fabulous, sumptuous, glittering tribute to the lofty ideal of romantic love'. A modern reading sees a self-pitying male lover romanticised while the women bear the costs.

how_they_meet: Chunnilal introduces Devdas to Chandramukhi at her kotha.
courtship_pattern: Chandramukhi falls in love with Devdas's tortured soul and turns her kotha into his sanctuary as his health fails; he remains devoted to Paro.
emotional_dynamic: Her selfless devotion against his unreachable grief
pair_conflict: Devdas's enduring love for Paro.
pair_friction_explanation: There is no hostility; the distance lies in Devdas's inability to return her love.
external_opposition_explanation: Her profession makes her a social outcast, and Kalibabu exposes her publicly at Paro's Durga Puja.
lover_boy_explanation: Devdas has no romantic identity towards Chandramukhi; she is his refuge, not his beloved.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Chandramukhi's devotion is met by Devdas's drunken indifference, so Dixit carries the relationship and the pairing works as pathos rather than mutual romance.
actor_transformation: Her kotha becomes his refuge as his health fails, but he does not transfer his love.
female_transformation: From glamorous courtesan to selfless companion who publicly defends her dignity.
relationship_outcome: Devdas leaves her to die at Paro's gate.
relationship_analysis: Chandramukhi is the film's ideal of selfless love: she asks nothing and gives sanctuary, and even Paro recognises her devotion. Her dance with Paro and her public defence of her dignity give her more presence than the novel's courtesan.
critical_reading: Madhuri Dixit's Chandramukhi drew the most praise from Indian critics, while Deepak Gahlot objected to the invented meeting and dance between Paro and Chandramukhi. A modern reading sees the courtesan's worth measured by her self-sacrifice for an unresponsive man.

how_they_meet: Priya crashes her car into Raj's truck.
courtship_pattern: After a rocky start they meet again at a friends' wedding, become friends and fall in love; Raj follows the engaged Priya to Greece and woos her until she realises she loves him, and they marry after persuading her parents.
emotional_dynamic: Opposites attracted; in marriage, love expressed through constant arguing
pair_conflict: Financial strain and her family's expectations; Priya secretly borrows from her former fiancé, and Raj accuses her of infidelity.
pair_friction_explanation: The marriage is marked by constant arguments, and Raj's accusation of infidelity drives Priya to her parents and nearly to Greece.
external_opposition_explanation: Priya's engagement to Sameer stands in the way at first; later her family's expectations and insults add to Raj's financial pressure.
lover_boy_explanation: Raj is a devoted romantic hero who pursues Priya to Greece and vows never to give up on their love, though insecurity makes him a difficult husband.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The marriage drama depends on Khan and Mukerji's quarrels feeling like those of a real couple, and their volatile rapport makes the strain credible.
actor_transformation: Recognises his insecurity, promises to change and holds to his vow never to give up on their love.
female_transformation: From a planner from a wealthy family to a wife who chooses the difficult marriage over escape.
relationship_outcome: Priya returns home to Raj; they keep arguing, which they call their way of expressing love.
relationship_analysis: Chalte Chalte carries Khan's romance past the wedding. The courtship follows the familiar pursuit of an engaged woman, but the second half is about class pressure, money and pride inside a marriage. The ending recasts their fights as love rather than resolving their causes.
critical_reading: Taran Adarsh wrote that the film 'clearly belongs to Shah Rukh Khan'; some critics noted its similarity to Saathiya. A modern reading credits its attention to post-marital conflict but notes that the hero's infidelity accusation is quickly forgiven.

how_they_meet: Aman and his mother move in next door to Naina's family in New York.
courtship_pattern: Aman's cheer transforms Naina's family and she falls in love with him. Secretly terminally ill, he lets her believe he is married, steers her towards Rohit, and confesses his feelings only by reading them as Rohit's from Rohit's diary.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual love suppressed by his secret illness
pair_conflict: Aman's concealment of his heart condition and his matchmaking.
pair_friction_explanation: Aman's deception wounds Naina twice, when she sees the 'wedding' photograph and when she discovers his scheme, but it is protective rather than hostile.
external_opposition_explanation: Aman's fatal heart condition makes a future impossible, and Naina's engagement to Rohit follows from his plan.
lover_boy_explanation: Aman's love for Naina drives his final months and ends in the ultimate romantic sacrifice.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Aman's playful courting of Naina, then his withdrawal, is the film's emotional engine, and Khan and Zinta make both the teasing and the renunciation convincing.
actor_transformation: From a cheerful fixer of others' lives to a dying man who gives up his own love for Naina's future.
female_transformation: From a pessimistic, uptight student to a woman who learns to live fully.
relationship_outcome: Naina marries Rohit; Aman dies after making Rohit promise that Naina will be his in the next life.
relationship_analysis: KHNH is Khan's definitive self-sacrificing lover: Aman loves Naina but hides his illness, fakes a marriage and voices his own feelings as Rohit's. The film makes renunciation the highest proof of love, and his death leaves the romance permanently unfulfilled.
critical_reading: Komal Nahta called Aman 'one of the best roles of his career' and Jitesh Pillai called Khan 'the soul' of the film, while Rama Sharma (The Tribune) found him 'overcharged' at times. A modern reading notes that Aman decides Naina's future for her.

how_they_meet: Posing as a college student, Ram meets Chandni, his chemistry professor.
courtship_pattern: Ram falls in love with Chandni; together they give Sanjana a makeover, and he foils an attempt to abduct Chandni at the prom.
emotional_dynamic: Comic infatuation within an undercover mission
pair_conflict: His undercover identity.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between them is recorded beyond the concealment of his identity.
external_opposition_explanation: Raghavan's gang tries to abduct Chandni and later holds the college hostage.
lover_boy_explanation: Ram's mission and family reconciliation come first; the romance is a comic strand that plays with Khan's romantic image.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Ram's comic infatuation with his teacher is staged as fantasy and slapstick, and Sen plays along well enough to make it one of the film's lighter pleasures.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: Learns that Ram is an army officer.
relationship_outcome: Not documented beyond Chandni discovering his true identity.
relationship_analysis: The romance is a comic sideline in a film about Ram's mission and his reconciliation with his stepmother and half-brother. Its premise, an army major posing as a student who falls for his teacher, plays Khan's romantic persona for comedy. Chandni first treats Ram's attention as a joke but comes to return it, which makes the attraction mutual by the end.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Veer, an Indian Air Force pilot, rescues Zaara after her bus crashes in India.
courtship_pattern: He helps her scatter her nanny's ashes and takes her to his village for Lohri; at the station he confesses his love to the engaged Zaara. When her friend Shabbo calls, he quits the Air Force and goes to Pakistan to bring her away.
emotional_dynamic: Idealised mutual devotion across a national border
pair_conflict: None between them; Veer agrees to leave to protect her family's honour.
pair_friction_explanation: The lovers are aligned throughout; their separations are imposed or chosen for each other's sake.
external_opposition_source: Family; Existing relationship; War or politics; Distance
external_opposition_explanation: Zaara's political family and her fiancé Raza oppose the match; Raza has Veer jailed as an Indian spy for 22 years while the world believes him dead.
lover_boy_explanation: A defining lover-boy role: Veer gives up his career and 22 years of freedom for Zaara.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The film's decades-spanning devotion rests on Khan and Zinta's tenderness in the early Punjab scenes, which remains the reference point for the later separation.
actor_transformation: Gives up his career and, silently, 22 years of freedom to protect Zaara's life and reputation.
female_transformation: Breaks her engagement, leaves Pakistan and devotes her life to Veer's village.
relationship_outcome: Freed after 22 years, Veer marries Zaara and they cross back into India together.
relationship_analysis: Veer-Zaara is Khan's purest sacrificial lover: Veer accepts 22 years of silent imprisonment rather than a scandal that would harm Zaara, and she, believing him dead, builds her life around his dream. The couple never quarrels; the obstacles are a jealous fiancé, a political family and the India–Pakistan divide, which the film resolves as a plea for reconciliation.
critical_reading: Critics praised the story, music, performances and 'sensitive portrayal of India-Pakistan relations'; Deepu Madhavan (NDTV) called it 'an ode to ageless romance', while Sukanya Verma and Teena Malik criticised its repetition of Chopra formulae. A modern reading admires its restraint but notes that the heroine's life is organised around a man presumed dead.

how_they_meet: Childhood friends who reconnect when Mohan comes to Charanpur to find his nanny Kaveri Amma.
courtship_pattern: Gita first resents Mohan; drawn to her progressive ideals, he joins her campaign for the education of girls and lower-caste children, and they grow close. She asks him to move to India permanently.
emotional_dynamic: Initial resentment turning into shared purpose and affection
pair_conflict: Gita's fear that Mohan will take Kaveri Amma away, and his divided commitment between NASA and India.
pair_friction_explanation: Gita's early resentment and their disagreement over where Mohan belongs are real but civil.
external_opposition_explanation: Mohan's career ties him to the United States, and caste and religious prejudice obstruct the causes that bring them together.
lover_boy_explanation: Mohan's arc is his return to India and service to the village; the romance is understated.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Mohan and Gita's relationship grows from argument to respect, and the restrained playing by Khan and debutante Joshi suits the film's realism.
actor_transformation: Her commitment to her homeland helps draw Mohan back to India for good.
female_transformation: Not documented beyond her steadfast work for the village.
relationship_outcome: Mohan resigns from NASA and returns to India.
relationship_analysis: Gita is less a romantic prize than the embodiment of the film's argument: her school and her refusal to leave India make her the voice of the homeland Mohan must choose. The romance is understated and bound up with civic purpose.
critical_reading: Swades received universal acclaim, and Khan's performance is considered one of his best. A modern reading values a heroine whose agency and ideals precede the hero's arrival.

how_they_meet: A ghost at a dharamshala is captivated by Lachchi as her wedding party rests on the way to her in-laws' village.
courtship_pattern: After her husband leaves on their wedding night, the ghost takes his form, reveals his true identity to Lachchi and wins her with a sensual, magical, self-confident love.
emotional_dynamic: Attentive devotion that fulfils the desires her husband ignored
pair_conflict: None between them; the deception of the family and the real Kishanlal's return threaten them.
pair_friction_explanation: The ghost is honest with Lachchi and she chooses him knowingly; no conflict between them is recorded.
external_opposition_explanation: The real Kishanlal returns, the rival Thakurs press the family to find the truth, and the shepherd traps the ghost in a bottle.
lover_boy_explanation: The ghost exists as a lover: he takes a human form out of love and finally enters the bottle solely to prove it.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The ghost's courtship of Lachchi is played as gentle fantasy, and Khan and Mukerji give it warmth within the folk-tale frame.
actor_transformation: Proves his love by entering the bottle and, in the twist ending, possesses Kishanlal's body to stay with Lachchi.
female_transformation: From an abandoned bride to a woman who knowingly chooses love and bears the ghost's child.
relationship_outcome: The ghost escapes the bottle and lives with Lachchi in Kishanlal's body.
relationship_analysis: Paheli gives Khan both halves of a marriage: the dutiful husband who abandons his bride for business and the ghost who offers her the love he withholds. Lachchi's knowing choice of the ghost legitimises female desire within a folk-tale frame, and the twist lets love triumph over propriety.
critical_reading: Taran Adarsh called Paheli 'one of the finest films produced in recent times'. A modern reading praises the film for centring a wife's choice, though the resolution depends on possessing her husband's body.

how_they_meet: An arranged marriage between families from distant villages.
courtship_pattern: None: on their wedding night Kishanlal turns away to finish his bookkeeping and leaves at dawn on a five-year business trip.
emotional_dynamic: Duty to his father placed above his bride
pair_conflict: His neglect and absence.
pair_friction_explanation: Kishanlal's abandonment devastates Lachchi, and on his return he disputes her double's claim, but no quarrel between them is described.
external_opposition_explanation: His father's wish that he start a business on an auspicious date takes him away.
lover_boy_explanation: Kishanlal is the opposite of a lover boy: a workaholic son indifferent to his bride.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Kishanlal's coldness towards Lachchi is the point, so the real marriage is played without warmth by design.
actor_transformation: Returns on hearing that his wife is pregnant, proves he is the real husband, and is then possessed by the ghost.
female_transformation: Turns from her absent husband to the ghost.
relationship_outcome: Identified as the real Kishanlal, he is possessed by the ghost.
relationship_analysis: Kishanlal is the anti-lover of Khan's filmography: a son so dutiful and a merchant so diligent that he leaves his bride untouched. His failure is what makes the ghost's romance possible and sympathetic.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Dev meets Maya by chance on her wedding day; they form an immediate connection, and as he leaves he is hit by a car.
courtship_pattern: Four years later their elders' friendship brings them together; they bond over their unhappy marriages, try to help each other repair them, then confess their love at a train station and begin an affair.
emotional_dynamic: Two unhappy spouses finding recognition in each other, shadowed by guilt
pair_conflict: Guilt towards their spouses and families; later, Dev's belief that Maya has returned to Rishi.
pair_friction_explanation: The lovers are aligned; the strain is guilt, their decision to separate and Dev's avoidance of Maya at the station.
external_opposition_explanation: Both are married; their families discover the affair, Sam dies of a heart attack that night, and both marriages end in divorce.
lover_boy_explanation: Dev becomes a romantic lead, but he begins as a bitter, resentful husband and the film dwells on his guilt.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; Taran Adarsh (Bollywood Hungama) praised the chemistry among the cast. The affair works because Khan and Mukerji make the two unhappy spouses' attraction feel adult and conflicted.
actor_transformation: From a bitter, resentful husband to a man who confesses his affair and, years later, reunites with Maya.
female_transformation: From an emotionally distant wife to a divorced woman who chooses to find Dev.
relationship_outcome: After their divorces and three years apart, they reunite on a departing train.
relationship_analysis: KANK is Khan's most direct romance of adultery: Dev is not a lover boy but an injured, resentful husband whose love for Maya grows out of shared marital failure. The film refuses to make either spouse a villain, and its happy ending is weighed down by guilt.
critical_reading: Critics praised its bold treatment of infidelity and its performances but criticised its length and melodrama; it has since been called ahead of its time. A modern reading credits its refusal to villainise the spouses.

how_they_meet: Not documented; they are married with a son when the film begins.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable: an established marriage.
emotional_dynamic: Dev's resentment of Rhea's success against her efforts to hold the family together
pair_conflict: Dev's insecurity and detachment after his injury, the London promotion Rhea turns down, and his affair.
pair_friction_explanation: Dev accuses Rhea of self-centredness; she confronts his resentment; the marriage ends when he confesses his affair.
external_opposition_explanation: The pressure comes from Dev's lost career and Rhea's rising one rather than from outsiders.
lover_boy_explanation: Dev is a detached, jealous husband with no romantic function towards Rhea.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; Taran Adarsh's praise of the cast's chemistry is general. Dev and Rhea's marriage is written as failing, and the two play distance more than intimacy.
actor_transformation: Confesses the affair and loses the marriage.
female_transformation: From a wife who gives up a promotion for her family to a divorced mother who moves on with her boss Jai.
relationship_outcome: Divorced; Rhea dates Jai and encourages Maya to find Dev.
relationship_analysis: Rhea is written with unusual sympathy: the successful wife whose sacrifices go unseen by a husband resentful of her career. Her grace in urging Maya to find Dev lets the film end without a villain.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Roma infiltrates Don's gang to avenge her brother Ramesh, whom Don killed.
courtship_pattern: She tries to kill 'Don', learns he is the lookalike Vijay, and allies with him to recover the disc; after the showdown 'Vijay' returns her declared love, but a line Don once said to her reveals who he is.
emotional_dynamic: A vengeful infiltrator turned ally whose love is exploited
pair_conflict: Don murdered her brother; the man she loves is Don in disguise.
pair_friction_explanation: Roma's feelings are for Vijay, but the man who accepts them is her brother's killer deceiving her.
external_opposition_explanation: The cartel war and Vardhaan's scheme drive the alliance and put both in danger.
lover_boy_explanation: Don uses romance as cover; there is no romantic devotion.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Roma's revenge mission keeps the relationship as wary cat-and-mouse, and Chopra and Khan play the tension rather than romance.
actor_transformation: None: Don's apparent redemption as Vijay is a masquerade.
female_transformation: From avenger to a woman who confesses love and realises too late that she has been played.
relationship_outcome: Don, posing as Vijay, accepts her love and becomes kingpin.
relationship_analysis: The romance is the bait for Don's final twist: Roma's love for the good lookalike is answered by her brother's killer. The double role lets the film offer, then withdraw, a redemptive romantic hero.
critical_reading: Taran Adarsh praised Priyanka Chopra's action scenes and Khan's Don; Sukanya Verma found Khan inconsistent in the dual roles. A modern reading notes that the heroine's agency in combat does not extend to seeing through the deception.

how_they_meet: Omi, a junior artist who worships the star Shanti, rescues her when she is trapped in a fire on set.
courtship_pattern: Omi first poses as a Tamil star, then confesses the truth; Shanti befriends him and they share an evening at the studio, until he learns she is secretly married to Mukesh and pregnant.
emotional_dynamic: A fan's worshipful love met with warm friendship
pair_conflict: Shanti's secret marriage to Mukesh.
pair_friction_explanation: Omi's initial lie is minor and confessed; the only strain is his heartbreak on discovering her marriage.
external_opposition_explanation: Shanti is married to Mukesh, who murders her and their unborn child in a fire that Omi fails to stop.
lover_boy_explanation: Omi's life is organised around his adoration of Shanti, and he dies trying to save her; the reborn Om avenges her.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Om's worship of the star is played with comic sincerity, and Padukone's debut gives the unattainable Shanti enough warmth for the reincarnation romance to carry.
actor_transformation: Dies trying to rescue her and, reborn as Om Kapoor, avenges her.
female_transformation: Her ghost returns to bring about Mukesh's death and find peace.
relationship_outcome: Shanti is murdered; Omi dies trying to save her; his reincarnation and her ghost together avenge her before she departs.
relationship_analysis: Om Shanti Om turns the star-crossed romance into a love letter to Hindi cinema: Omi's devotion is a fan's love for a screen idol, unrequited in life and fulfilled only as justice across rebirth. Shanti's ghost, not the reborn hero alone, completes the revenge.
critical_reading: A reviewer called the film a 'valentine to the movies', and critics praised Khan and Padukone's debut. A modern reading notes that the heroine's story is told through her murder and her ghost.

initial_relationship: Strangers; he loves her from afar
how_they_meet: Suri, an employee of Punjab Power, falls for Taani, his former professor's daughter, during preparations for her wedding.
courtship_pattern: After her fiancé dies, her dying father asks Suri to marry her; she agrees out of respect but says she cannot love him. Unable to express himself as Suri, he adopts the flamboyant persona Raj, becomes her dance partner and confesses his love as Raj.
emotional_dynamic: A shy husband's silent devotion; a lively wife drawn to his disguised alter ego
pair_conflict: Taani's inability to love Suri and her attraction to 'Raj'.
pair_friction_explanation: Taani tells Suri she cannot love him and nearly elopes with Raj, but there is no hostility; Suri treats her kindly throughout.
external_opposition_explanation: Her fiancé's death and her father's fatal heart attack force the marriage on both of them.
lover_boy_explanation: A defining lover-boy role: Suri's every action, including inventing Raj, is aimed at winning his wife's love.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The double identity splits the chemistry: Suri's shy devotion and Raj's brash flirting, with Sharma's debut performance making Taani's confusion credible.
actor_transformation: The shy clerk invents a flamboyant alter ego to court his own wife and is finally loved as himself.
female_transformation: From a grieving bride who cannot love her husband to a wife who recognises his devotion and returns it.
relationship_outcome: Taani realises Raj is Suri, accepts him, and they win the competition and leave for a honeymoon in Japan.
relationship_analysis: RNBDJ literalises Khan's two screen selves: the ordinary, devoted husband and the flamboyant romantic hero. The film argues that Taani should love the plain man, yet wins her through the fantasy persona and a disguise that tests her fidelity; she chooses her marriage before she knows the truth.
critical_reading: Robert Abele (Los Angeles Times) found Khan's Sellers-to-Jerry Lewis transformation 'agreeably amusing' and Frank Lovece called it 'smarter and more self-aware of its rom-com contrivances than most Hollywood movies'; Derek Elley (Variety) mocked the 'huge credibility gap' of Taani never recognising him. A modern reading notes that the disguise works as a loyalty test the wife never agreed to.

how_they_meet: Selling his brother's beauty products in San Francisco, Rizwan meets Mandira, a Hindu single mother working as a hairstylist.
courtship_pattern: Rizwan falls in love with Mandira and marries her despite his brother Zakir's disapproval of an interfaith match; she and her son Sam take the Khan surname.
emotional_dynamic: Rizwan's literal, unconditional devotion met with warmth, then shattered by grief
pair_conflict: After Sam is killed in an Islamophobic attack, Mandira blames the Khan name and sends Rizwan away.
pair_friction_explanation: Mandira's grief turns on Rizwan and she drives him out with a sarcastic demand he takes literally: a serious rupture, though born of loss rather than hostility.
external_opposition_explanation: Zakir opposes the interfaith marriage; post-9/11 Islamophobia leads to Sam's killing, Rizwan's arrest and his stabbing by an extremist.
lover_boy_explanation: Devotion to Mandira drives Rizwan's cross-country quest, but his autism and his stand against prejudice define the role as much as romance.
chemistry_explanation: Taran Adarsh called Kajol the actress with 'the strongest chemistry' with Khan, and Savera R. Gupta (The Telegraph) welcomed their reunion. Interpretive score.
actor_transformation: Takes Mandira's demand literally and crosses America to tell the President he is not a terrorist, becoming a national figure.
female_transformation: From a joyful wife to a grieving mother who blames her husband, then seeks justice for Sam and returns to Rizwan.
relationship_outcome: Mandira joins Rizwan in Georgia; after he survives a stabbing and meets President Obama, they return home together.
relationship_analysis: MNIK makes the Khan–Kajol pairing the vessel of a political parable: the interfaith marriage embodies the tolerance that post-9/11 Islamophobia destroys. Rizwan's devotion is literal and unconditional, and his quest to clear the family name is also a quest to win back his wife.
critical_reading: Critics praised the lead performances, and Taran Adarsh called Khan's his career best; Shubhra Gupta (The Indian Express) felt the push to make Rizwan more heroic derailed the film's arc. A modern reading notes that the heroine's grief is framed as a wrong the hero must heal.

how_they_meet: Not documented; they are married with a son, Prateek, when the film begins.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable: after Shekhar's death, G.One, who wears his face, promises Sonia to protect their son, and she cannot bring herself to leave him behind.
emotional_dynamic: A loving marriage cut short, echoed in Sonia's bond with the digital hero who bears her husband's face
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between Shekhar and Sonia is recorded; low score carries Low confidence.
external_opposition_explanation: Ra.One kills Shekhar, later hypnotises Sonia, takes her form and sends her to crash a train.
lover_boy_explanation: Shekhar is a father and game designer, and G.One a protector; romance is a faint undertone.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The marriage is affectionate but sketched, and the film spends more time on Sonia's bond with G.One than with Shekhar.
actor_transformation: Shekhar dies trying to protect his son; G.One, bearing his face, becomes the family's protector.
female_transformation: A grieving widow who comes to trust G.One and is saved from the train crash.
relationship_outcome: Shekhar is killed; G.One saves Sonia and Prateek, disintegrates, and is later restored by Prateek.
relationship_analysis: The marriage exists mainly to be lost and partly recovered: Shekhar's death leaves Sonia and Prateek with a machine that has his face, and the film hints at, without pursuing, a displaced romance between the widow and the superhero. The marriage itself is shown as affectionate on both sides, with Sonia exasperated by but fond of Shekhar.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Continuing from Don (2006): Roma, now with Interpol, receives Don's surrender in Malaysia.
courtship_pattern: None: Roma pursues Don across Europe and, in a standoff, cannot bring herself to kill him.
emotional_dynamic: Suppressed attraction beneath professional enmity
pair_conflict: Don killed her brother, and she is sworn to bring him to justice.
pair_friction_explanation: They are adversaries: Roma hunts Don for his crimes, and her feelings survive only as reluctance to kill him outside the law.
external_opposition_explanation: The European cartel, Vardhaan and the hit man Jabbar turn the standoff violent; Jabbar shoots Roma.
lover_boy_explanation: Don is a criminal mastermind; his only romantic gesture is getting the wounded Roma to an ambulance.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Roma remains Don's adversary, and the hint of attraction is played as tension within the heist rather than as romance.
actor_transformation: None; Don remains a criminal, though he ensures Roma reaches an ambulance.
female_transformation: From avenger to Interpol officer who refuses to kill Don illegally despite her feelings.
relationship_outcome: Roma is shot by Jabbar and taken to an ambulance; Don escapes as king of the underworld.
relationship_analysis: Don 2 keeps the romance as an undercurrent: Roma's lingering feelings for her brother's killer are tested when she will not shoot him outside the law. Don's care for her wound is the film's only concession to romance.
critical_reading: Rachit Gupta (Filmfare, 4/5) credited Khan, Chopra and Irani with carrying the film. A modern reading notes that the heroine's integrity is framed through her attraction to the villain.

how_they_meet: Samar, working part-time as a waiter in London, meets Meera at her engagement party to Roger.
courtship_pattern: They trade Punjabi lessons for English lessons, fall in love after a night of street dancing, and Samar reconciles Meera with her estranged mother; she decides to break off her engagement.
emotional_dynamic: Exuberant love overshadowed by her bargains with God
pair_conflict: After Samar's accident Meera vows never to see him again if his life is spared; later, his ultimatum that she be with him or watch him risk death.
pair_friction_explanation: Meera's vow and Samar's furious departure cause a ten-year rupture, and their second confrontation ends with his ultimatum.
external_opposition_explanation: Meera's engagement to Roger stands in the way, and two accidents shape the lovers' separation and reunion.
lover_boy_explanation: Samar's life is organised around Meera: first courtship, then a decade of daring death to defeat her vow.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The London romance has the classic Yash Chopra staging, but the vow-driven separation and Meera's restraint leave the pairing more earnest than electric.
actor_transformation: From a cheerful London street musician to an embittered bomb-disposal officer challenging God to kill him, and back to love.
female_transformation: From a woman bound by her bargains with God to one who believes God wants people to love and be happy.
relationship_outcome: Meera travels to Kashmir; Samar defuses his last bomb and proposes.
relationship_analysis: Yash Chopra's last film pits romantic love against religious bargaining: Meera's vows separate the lovers, and Samar's answer is to court death daily. The conflict is genuinely between the couple, and its resolution requires the heroine to revise her faith rather than the hero to change.
critical_reading: Taran Adarsh (4/5) found the complex love story more gripping as it went on, and Shabana Ansari (DNA) said Khan 'can still convey love and passion in a fleeting look'. A modern reading sees Samar's ultimatum as emotional coercion.

how_they_meet: Samar rescues Akira, a Discovery Channel filmmaker, after she dives into Pangong Lake, leaving his jacket and diary with her.
courtship_pattern: After reading his diary she films his bomb-disposal squad and falls for him; he does not reciprocate because he still loves Meera.
emotional_dynamic: Akira's admiration against Samar's closed heart
pair_conflict: Samar's unresolved love for Meera.
pair_friction_explanation: Samar gently rebuffs Akira; they remain close collaborators.
external_opposition_explanation: Samar's enduring love for Meera is the only obstacle.
lover_boy_explanation: Samar has no romantic identity towards Akira.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Akira's brash flirtation with the older soldier gives the film its liveliest banter, and Sharma's energy plays well against Khan's reserve.
actor_transformation: Her documentary draws Samar back to London, leading to the accident and his reunion with Meera.
female_transformation: From an impulsive filmmaker infatuated with Samar to the woman who reunites him with Meera.
relationship_outcome: Akira bids farewell as Meera goes to Samar.
relationship_analysis: Akira is the modern, forthright counterpart to Meera's faith-bound reserve. Her love goes unreturned, but she becomes the engine of the lovers' reunion.
critical_reading: Anushka Sharma was one of the film's main award winners, though some critics' spoof awards nominated both her and Kaif. No reading of the pair itself was found.

how_they_meet: Rahul helps Meenamma and her four cousins board the moving Chennai Express, a spoof of the train scene in Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge.
courtship_pattern: Meenamma presents Rahul as her lover to escape a forced marriage; they flee together, quarrel, pose as a married couple in a village and scatter his grandfather's ashes, and Rahul takes her home to fight for her.
emotional_dynamic: Comic bickering across a language barrier turning to love
pair_conflict: Rahul's reluctance and repeated attempts to escape.
pair_friction_explanation: They quarrel and part ways once, and Rahul keeps trying to leave, but the conflict is largely comic.
external_opposition_explanation: Her father, a powerful crime boss, has fixed her marriage to the gangster Tangaballi, whose men and sickle-wielding henchmen pursue the couple.
lover_boy_explanation: Rahul begins as an unheroic, reluctant bachelor and earns lover-hero status only at the climax, in a self-parody of Khan's romantic image.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The road-comedy sparring between Rahul and Meenamma drives the film, and Padukone's comic timing matches Khan's, making the bickering read as attraction.
actor_transformation: From a self-centred bachelor to a 'common man' who takes Tangaballi's blows for love.
female_transformation: From a fugitive bride who uses Rahul to a woman whose choice her father accepts.
relationship_outcome: Rahul defeats Tangaballi and Durgesh allows him to marry Meenamma.
relationship_analysis: Chennai Express turns Khan's romantic iconography into comedy: the DDLJ train scene is spoofed at the outset, and the reluctant Rahul must earn the heroism his persona once assumed. The romance also stages a North–South language and culture gap that love is said to overcome.
critical_reading: Reviews were mixed. A modern reading notes that humour at the expense of Tamil speech and customs sits uneasily with the film's message that love knows no regional barriers.

how_they_meet: Nandu enlists Mohini, a bar dancer, to train the team for the World Dance Championship.
courtship_pattern: Mohini develops feelings for Charlie while training the team; he reveals the heist and his father's suicide, she joins the plan, and at the opening of her dance school he proposes with a ring made from one of the diamonds.
emotional_dynamic: Her feelings for a man consumed by revenge
pair_conflict: Charlie's concealment of the heist and Mohini's refusal to abandon the finals.
pair_friction_explanation: The heist secret and Mohini's decision to dance rather than flee split the group, but the couple is reconciled on stage.
external_opposition_explanation: Grover's scheming threatens the team but not the romance directly.
lover_boy_explanation: Charlie is driven by revenge; the romance is a late addition.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Mohini's dance lessons give the pair some charm, but the heist-ensemble format keeps the romance secondary and broad.
actor_transformation: Revenge gives way to shared triumph and a proposal.
female_transformation: From bar dancer to champion and dance-school owner whose integrity changes the team's plan.
relationship_outcome: Charlie proposes to Mohini with a diamond ring at her school's opening.
relationship_analysis: The romance is decorative in a heist caper, though Mohini's insistence on dancing for India turns the gang's escape into the film's patriotic climax.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: In Sofia, Kaali meets Meera during one of his gang's chases with his father's rival, Dev Malik.
courtship_pattern: Kaali falls for Meera; she reveals herself as Malik's daughter and spares him, then declares her love after he saves her from falling off a cliff. When their fathers kill each other she believes Kaali betrayed her and shoots him. Fifteen years later their younger siblings' romance brings them together again.
emotional_dynamic: Passionate love shattered by a misread betrayal
pair_conflict: Meera's belief that Kaali killed her father.
pair_friction_explanation: Meera shoots Kaali and later tries to keep her sister from his brother; the rift lasts fifteen years until she learns the truth.
external_opposition_explanation: Their fathers are warring crime bosses who die in a shootout, and the drug baron King's attack nearly kills Meera.
lover_boy_explanation: Kaali is a romantic hero in both timelines, though the family and gangster plots share the film.
chemistry_explanation: Reviewers praised the Khan–Kajol chemistry; Shubha Shetty-Saha (Mid-Day) said it 'refuses to simmer down even after all these years'. Interpretive score.
actor_transformation: From a crime boss's son to a car mechanic hiding his past, who fights again as Kaali to protect his family.
female_transformation: From a gangster's daughter who shoots her lover to a woman who apologises and takes a bullet for him.
relationship_outcome: Meera takes King's bullet for Raj, recovers and reunites with him.
relationship_analysis: Dilwale trades on the Khan–Kajol legacy, but its romance is built on mistrust: the lovers are children of warring gangsters, and a single misread moment makes Meera shoot Kaali. Reconciliation requires her apology and sacrifice.
critical_reading: Critics praised the chemistry while criticising the screenplay and runtime (20% on Rotten Tomatoes). A modern reading notes that the heroine carries the burden of error and atonement.

how_they_meet: Sejal, a Gujarati lawyer who loses her engagement ring on a European tour, stays behind and enlists Harry, her family's guide, to retrace her steps.
courtship_pattern: Their bickering turns into closeness across Europe; Sejal hides that she has found the ring to prolong the trip, Harry refuses to cross a line with her, and after she flies home he follows her to India, where her wedding has been called off.
emotional_dynamic: A cynical, lonely womaniser and a headstrong, naive traveller draw out each other's vulnerability
pair_conflict: Harry's inferiority complex and refusal to admit his feelings; Sejal's engagement.
pair_friction_explanation: Constant bickering and a heated argument over where they stand lead Sejal to go home; the conflict is Harry's evasion rather than hostility.
external_opposition_explanation: Sejal's engagement to Rupen and her family's call to return to India separate them.
lover_boy_explanation: Harry is a romantic lead whose healing comes through love, though he begins as a jaded womaniser and hesitates until the end.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. The travelogue romance depends on the leads' banter, which Khan and Sharma keep likeable even where the script meanders.
actor_transformation: From a rootless womaniser hiding homesickness to a man who declares his love and returns to his village.
female_transformation: From a sheltered fiancée to a woman who chooses her own partner.
relationship_outcome: They decide to marry and visit Harry's family in Nurmahal.
relationship_analysis: Imtiaz Ali casts Khan as a jaded outsider who must be healed by love, yet keeps him chaste with the woman he loves. The real obstacle is Harry's sense of unworthiness more than Sejal's fiancé, and the romance doubles as his homecoming.
critical_reading: Anupama Chopra wrote that Imtiaz Ali could not fit Khan's persona to his own bruised brand of romance: 'Twenty-two years later, Shah Rukh is still Raj – tender, sensitive and resolutely chaste'. A modern reading sees a romance that promises moral complexity but reverts to the chaste lover-boy ideal.

how_they_meet: Through matrimonial agencies, Bauua, a short man from Meerut, finds Aafia, a scientist with cerebral palsy.
courtship_pattern: They fall in love, but Bauua dumps her after five months; when Aafia seeks him out their parents fix the marriage, and he flees the wedding to win a contest to meet the star Babita.
emotional_dynamic: Aafia's steady love against Bauua's immaturity and insecurity
pair_conflict: Bauua's abandonment of Aafia, twice.
pair_friction_explanation: Bauua abandons Aafia after five months and again on their wedding day; she later refuses to see him.
external_opposition_explanation: Bauua's fixation on Babita, Aafia's engagement to her colleague Srinivasan, and his Mars mission keep them apart.
lover_boy_explanation: Bauua becomes a devoted lover only after failing Aafia; much of the role is comic bravado and self-redemption.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Bauua's brashness against Aafia's dignity gives the pair friction and some tenderness, though the abandonment plot undercuts it.
actor_transformation: From a brash, insecure man who flees commitment to one who volunteers for Mars and declares he always loved her.
female_transformation: From a woman who seeks marriage while pregnant to one who rejects Bauua, nearly marries another man, and rushes to see him off.
relationship_outcome: Aafia reaches the launch moments before take-off; after fifteen years lost in space, Bauua's pod returns to Earth.
relationship_analysis: Zero gives Khan his least idealised lover in years: Bauua abandons a disabled partner twice and chases a film star before trying to earn Aafia back with an absurdly grand gesture. The film leans on Aafia's patience for pathos, and the resolution is suspended in space.
critical_reading: Critics praised Khan's energy but found the second half overwrought; Rajeev Masand felt it becomes 'an entirely different film'. A modern reading questions whether the film uses Aafia's disability to ennoble Bauua's redemption.

how_they_meet: Bauua wins a dance contest whose prize is meeting the star Babita Kumari.
courtship_pattern: Babita hires Bauua for his knack for reading people; he accompanies her on shoots and helps her patch up with her unfaithful ex-boyfriend Aditya, while she tries to make him see his wrong towards Aafia.
emotional_dynamic: A lonely star's dependence on a devoted fan-assistant
pair_conflict: Bauua's guilt over Aafia and Babita's attachment to Aditya.
pair_friction_explanation: Bauua starts an argument at Babita's party and she throws him out.
external_opposition_explanation: Babita's relationship with Aditya and Bauua's unfinished bond with Aafia.
lover_boy_explanation: The summary describes employment and companionship, not courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; no fetched review assesses this pairing. Babita's relationship with Bauua is companionship and employment rather than romance, so there is little romantic interplay to judge.
actor_transformation: Her invented story about her parents makes him recognise his wrong towards Aafia.
female_transformation: An alcoholic star who finally breaks with the unfaithful Aditya.
relationship_outcome: Babita throws Bauua out; she later watches his launch on television.
relationship_analysis: The lead calls this a love triangle, but the plot summary describes a detour of employment, companionship and a moral lesson rather than a romance; mutuality is not scored.
critical_reading: Critics widely called Babita Kaif's best performance. No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Narmada negotiates with Azad during his metro hijacking; later her daughter Suji, looking for a husband for her mother, is impressed by Azad and arranges a meeting.
courtship_pattern: After sharing their views they get engaged and marry, while Narmada is unaware that her husband is the hijacker she is hunting.
emotional_dynamic: Mutual understanding shadowed by his double life
pair_conflict: Azad's secret identity as the vigilante Narmada is pursuing.
pair_friction_explanation: The marriage rests on concealment, and Narmada discovers her husband's alter ego after the wedding.
external_opposition_explanation: Kalee's brother uncovers the secret, and the couple are captured and tortured.
lover_boy_explanation: Azad's mission dominates; the marriage is a subplot.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; Manjusha Radhakrishnan (Gulf News) praised the star power of Khan and Nayanthara. The pairing is shaped by deception and the action plot, leaving the romance brief.
actor_transformation: Not documented.
female_transformation: From Force One negotiator to a wife who uncovers the truth about Azad and Vikram by posing as an inmate.
relationship_outcome: Captured and tortured together, then freed; the summary does not describe the marriage afterwards.
relationship_analysis: The marriage is a plot device of the vigilante thriller: Azad weds the officer hunting him, and her discovery of his double life is a twist rather than a romantic crisis.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Not documented.
courtship_pattern: Not applicable: they are married when the flashback begins.
emotional_dynamic: Not documented
pair_conflict: None documented.
pair_friction_explanation: No conflict between the couple is recorded; low score carries Low confidence.
external_opposition_explanation: Kalee attacks the couple, throws Vikram from a plane and frames him as a traitor; Aishwarya is sentenced to death for killing three of Kalee's policemen.
lover_boy_explanation: Vikram is a commando whose marriage is backstory to the revenge plot.
chemistry_explanation: Interpretive reading; Manjusha Radhakrishnan (Gulf News) praised the chemistry between Khan and Padukone. The flashback marriage is short but carries the film's emotional weight.
actor_transformation: Vikram loses his memory and lives with a tribe for thirty years before recovering it and avenging her.
female_transformation: Kills three corrupt policemen, is sentenced to death, and charges her son with proving Vikram's innocence.
relationship_outcome: Aishwarya is hanged five years after Azad's birth; Vikram and Azad later hang Kalee.
relationship_analysis: Aishwarya's story is the origin of the vigilante plot: her execution and her last words to her son turn a lost marriage into a mission of justice, and Kalee is hanged as she was. The brief flashback shows a loving, equal marriage.
critical_reading: No reading of the pair was found.

how_they_meet: Hardy, an ex-soldier, arrives in Laltu to repay a debt to Manu's late brother, who saved his life.
courtship_pattern: Hardy commits to getting Manu to England, travels with her on the illegal 'donkey flight' and protects her from an aggressive sham-marriage groom; deported after refusing to lie in court, he is separated from her for 25 years. When she is dying he brings her home, confesses his lifelong love and proposes.
emotional_dynamic: Protective devotion and loyalty across a 25-year separation
pair_conflict: Hardy's refusal to falsely claim persecution, which splits them.
pair_friction_explanation: They take different paths in the London court, but no hostility between them is recorded.
external_opposition_explanation: Visa rules, the deadly migration route and deportation separate them; Manu's asylum status bars her return, and brain cancer kills her.
lover_boy_explanation: Hardy's lifelong love and sacrifice define the role, though it is expressed through protection and principle more than courtship.
chemistry_explanation: Monika Rawal Kukreja (Hindustan Times) praised Khan's and Pannu's performances but was displeased with their chemistry. Interpretive score.
actor_transformation: From a debt-paying stranger to a lifelong lover who keeps his promise to bring Manu home.
female_transformation: From a poor villager desperate to emigrate to a British citizen who chooses to die in her homeland.
relationship_outcome: Manu accepts Hardy's proposal and dies moments later.
relationship_analysis: Dunki recasts Khan's sacrificial lover in a migration drama: Hardy's devotion is expressed through protection and principle rather than courtship, and his patriotism separates him from Manu for 25 years. The proposal comes only at her deathbed.
critical_reading: Critics praised the leads, but Monika Rawal Kukreja found their chemistry lacking and Uday Bhatia (Mint Lounge) accused the film of grandstanding on migration. A modern reading notes that the romance is subordinated to the hero's patriotic stand.
